subjects.displayTitle: Business and finance: making trust visible
subjects.introduction: A single honestly earned coin can carry a value that a hoard of wrongful gain cannot match. From this starting point, the selections bring spiritual qualities into the practical details of commerce: protecting another person’s rights, defining a partnership, keeping accounts, meeting debts, resisting bribery, and exercising moderation. Leviticus similarly places the ordinary tools of exchange—weights and measures—within the obligations of religious life [1]. The neighboring subjects of gambling and prayer for justice widen the inquiry into the consequences of desire and the formation of fair judgment. These readings invite us to consider business as a field in which trust becomes observable, while holding together diligence, mutual benefit, and detachment from fluctuating fortunes.
subjects.arc: Begin with the worth of honest work, develop the obligations of fair dealing, and move through moderation, public integrity, and concrete accounts of commercial life.

subjects.displayTitle: Gambling and recreation: looking beyond the first moment
subjects.introduction: Pleasure in the present can conceal consequences that unfold later. These three selections distinguish innocent pastime from wasted time, urge attention to the outcome of an action, and state the prohibition of gambling. The Buddhist discourse to Sigāla also considers gambling through its effects on wealth, relationships, and trust [1]. Read alongside the counsels on moderation in business and action suited to circumstances, this short compilation invites reflection on how recreation can refresh life and how habits can gradually redirect it.
subjects.arc: Begin with the place of innocent recreation, look ahead to consequences, and conclude with the stated prohibition.

order.why: Start with the distinction between harmless pastime and its possible excess.
Ask the reader to look beyond immediate attraction toward consequences.
Read the prohibition within this wider concern for a person’s life and well-being.

questions: What helps a person recognize when a pastime is ceasing to refresh life and beginning to consume attention, time, or relationships?
How does the Buddhist account of consequences deepen the discussion of gambling, and what does the distinction between a general rule and the judgment of particular activities bring into view?

neighbors.invitation: Consider the preference for steady work over speculative excitement.
Explore the need to bring ideals into practicable judgment.

references.label: 1 · Dīgha Nikāya 31, Sigālovāda Sutta, the six consequences of gambling (Narada Thera translation)
references.note: The discourse describes gambling as a source of heedlessness and follows its effects into hostility, grief, loss, and damaged confidence in a person. Compare this attention to consequences with the selection about seeing beyond an action’s beginning. The discourse’s guidance for householders supplies its own Buddhist ethical setting; it does not define the scope of the Bahá’í law or classify every form of recreation.

subjects.displayTitle: Slavery: no servant of God is a commodity
subjects.introduction: The force of this brief passage lies in its reason as well as its prohibition: a person who is a servant of God cannot purchase another of God’s servants. Seneca’s appeal to the shared humanity of enslaved and free people offers a philosophical comparison, while stopping at humane treatment within slavery [1]. Read beside fair dealing and the refusal to harm others, the passage invites sustained attention to the implications of spiritual equality for human relationships.
subjects.arc: Read the prohibition together with the shared relationship to God that grounds it.

order.why: Keep the single passage intact so that the prohibition and its reason remain inseparable.

neighbors.invitation: Consider the obligation to protect people’s rights in every transaction.
Explore another statement that joins the worth of one person to that of humanity.

references.label: 1 · Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 47, §§1 and 10–13
references.note: Seneca reminds a slaveholder that enslaved people share his human origin, life, and vulnerability to fortune, and calls for kind treatment and companionship. His letter continues to address the relationship of master and slave. Place that moral appeal beside the Aqdas prohibition on buying and selling human beings, attending to the difference between recognizing humanity within an institution and forbidding the transaction itself.

subjects.displayTitle: Murder and physical harm: the worth of a single life
subjects.introduction: One life is placed beside the whole of humanity in the opening passage, making the refusal to harm another a matter of spiritual vision as well as conduct. The selections condemn bloodshed, injury, and religious violence, while also preserving passages about defense, intention, courts, and penalties. These different contexts need to remain in view as the reader considers personal restraint and public justice. Qur’án 5:32 offers a close comparison with the opening image, within a verse that also contains explicit qualifications [1]. Alongside prayers for justice and the proposed Supreme Tribunal, this compilation asks how the protection of life can shape relationships, the handling of conflict, and institutions charged with responding to wrongdoing.
subjects.arc: Open with the value of one life, examine the rejection of violence and religious hostility, and then face the distinct questions of intention, defense, and public penalties.

references.note: The verse recounts an ordinance for the Children of Israel, relating the killing or saving of one person to all humanity. It includes qualifications concerning killing in retribution for a life and corruption in the land; these should remain visible in any comparison. Read the whole verse beside the Báb’s address to the people of the Bayán, considering both the shared image of human worth and the distinct wording and setting.

subjects.displayTitle: The Supreme Tribunal: making peace answerable to justice
subjects.introduction: The hope for peace becomes a question of design when nations must settle a dispute they cannot resolve alone. These selections envision a representative tribunal with authority to adjudicate, supported by governments and peoples, and sustained by a growing public commitment to peace. They also preserve qualifications about the future institution’s relationships and development. Kant’s proposal for a lasting federation offers a comparison: ending one war is different from establishing conditions that prevent wars from recurring [1]. Read alongside prayer for peace, the refusal of bloodshed, and action responsive to circumstances, the compilation invites inquiry into how representation, judgment, enforceable decisions, and moral commitment might work together.
subjects.arc: Begin with the public will for peace, examine representation and the tribunal’s work, then consider enforcement, the wider commonwealth, and the limits of what the selections specify.

references.note: Kant distinguishes a treaty ending one war from a lasting league seeking to end war itself. Compare this reasoning with the compilation’s emphasis on binding judgments and collective enforcement. The shared aim of enduring peace does not make the institutional proposals identical.

subjects.displayTitle: Praying for justice: protection, accountability, and changed hearts
subjects.introduction: A prayer for justice can ask for the oppressed to be protected and for the oppressor to become capable of justice. Both movements appear here, together with lament, appeals for steadfastness, demands for accountability, and petitions for the removal of tyranny. The range deserves to be heard without smoothing away its tensions. Psalm 72 begins by asking that a ruler receive righteous judgment, defend the needy, and confront oppression [1]. Read alongside fair dealing, the prohibition of harm, and prayer for peace, these selections connect the inward formation of judgment with the public conditions in which people live. They invite the reader to consider what one asks to be changed in others, in institutions, and in oneself.
subjects.arc: Begin with the striking prayer for an oppressor’s transformation, hear the suffering that gives it urgency, and follow the appeals into public justice and personal truthfulness.

references.note: The psalm asks God to give the king righteous judgment so that he may defend the poor and needy and confront their oppressor. Compare its conjunction of prayer and public responsibility with the petitions for rulers, the oppressed, and those who practice tyranny. The royal setting differs from many of the situations represented in the compilation, while raising a shared question about how power should serve justice.

subjects.displayTitle: Praying for peace: learning to hold the whole world in care
subjects.introduction: Peace is given a human face here in anguished mothers, orphaned children, endangered elders, and people whose homes and lives are overwhelmed by war. The prayers widen that care to animals, religious communities, nations, and even those whose hearts must turn away from violence. They also ask that the people praying become servants and promoters of peace. The Buddhist discourse on loving-kindness offers a comparison through its cultivation of goodwill toward all living beings, including those near and far [1]. Alongside justice and the Supreme Tribunal, these selections suggest that peace concerns both the conditions of public life and the breadth of affection a person learns to sustain.
subjects.arc: Begin with those who suffer from war, widen the circle of compassion, and move toward transformed hearts, service, and the hope of a united human family.

references.note: The discourse joins upright conduct with goodwill extended to all beings, without exclusion, and asks that this recollection be sustained in daily life. Compare its breadth of care with the prayers for humanity and other creatures. The Buddhist cultivation of loving-kindness and these petitions addressed to God have different forms, even as both invite a widening concern beyond one’s immediate circle.

subjects.displayTitle: The needs of the time: wisdom that finds a way to act
subjects.introduction: Lighting a candle where people gather gives practical wisdom an image: purpose must find a fitting place, moment, and manner of expression. These selections consider changing conditions, the capacity of listeners, danger, discretion, and the difference between what is desirable and what can be done. Their closing passages also insist that durable solutions require spiritual principle, giving the collection a tension worth exploring rather than a license for mere convenience. Aristotle’s account of practical wisdom likewise joins deliberation about a good life with attention to particular circumstances [1]. Read beside business conduct and institutions for peace, this compilation asks how conviction can remain steady while its expression becomes responsive, discerning, and effective.
subjects.arc: Begin with purposeful action fitted to its setting, examine changing circumstances and concrete counsels, and conclude with the relationship between practical measures and spiritual principle.

references.label: 1 · Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, VI.5 and VI.7 (W. D. Ross translation)
references.note: Aristotle describes practical wisdom as sound deliberation concerning a good human life and emphasizes that action requires knowledge of particulars as well as general truths. Compare this account with the selections’ attention to time, place, capacity, and feasibility. His philosophical account and the compilation’s counsel within a life of faith have different foundations; the comparison helps ask what discerning action requires.
